pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 11–12 years

- **Topic:** White Light & Colour

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS3 Physics, 'Light waves'):** "colours and the different frequencies of light, white light and prisms (qualitative only); differential colour effects in absorption and diffuse reflection." This is the DIRECT statutory home for the topic — spectrum/frequency, prism dispersion of white light (qualitative), and why objects appear coloured (selective absorption + diffuse reflection) all sit at KS3.

- **Standards — US (NGSS MS-PS4-2):** "[curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-PS4-2]." Colour is the WAVELENGTH-SELECTIVE case of this — a red object reflects red and absorbs the rest — so MS-PS4-2 is the honest national anchor, though NGSS has NO colour-specific performance expectation; the spectrum/dispersion and subtractive-colour detail are UK-led.

- **Operational details:** White light is a MIXTURE of all visible colours (ROYGBIV; red = lowest frequency/longest wavelength → violet = highest frequency/shortest). A PRISM disperses white light because different frequencies refract by different amounts (violet bends most, red least) — dispersion RESTS ON refraction (the hard prereq); a second prism recombines the spectrum back to white, proving white = all colours together. Objects appear coloured by SELECTIVE ABSORPTION: a red apple in white light absorbs most frequencies and reflects red to the eye; white reflects all, black absorbs all. Apparent colour depends on BOTH the pigment AND the illuminating light — a red object looks red in white light but BLACK in pure blue light (no red present to reflect). Filters are colour SUBTRACTORS: a red filter transmits red and absorbs the rest (it does NOT dye all light red); a coloured object is itself a selective filter. Present 'black' as the idealised limiting case (real pigments/lights give 'very dark', not perfectly black).

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B (transitional/early-formal). The qualitative model (absorb some, reflect the rest; light + pigment together) is age-appropriate, but SUBTRACTIVE reasoning is documented as genuinely hard even for motivated secondary students (only ~27% correctly predict a yellow object looks dark under blue light). Success = list ROYGBIV by frequency, explain prism dispersion via differential refraction, predict AND explain a red object going black under blue light, and predict the colour seen through a filter. Watch for colour-as-innate-property, light-just-brightens, and filter-as-adder thinking.
bestPractices: Use the IOP 'Wrong Track / Right Lines' refutation explicitly: name the intuition ('the dress is red and the light just brightens it up') and contrast it with the model ('white light falls, the dress absorbs most frequencies and reflects red to your eye') — a refutation-text move that outperforms simple telling.

Secure 'what IS white light' FIRST (Haagen-Schützenhöfer): pupils conceive white light as 'normal light', which blocks colour understanding — use a prism to split white light AND a second prism to RECOMBINE it, so white = all colours together is seen, not asserted.

Run predict-observe-reconcile with coloured light: pupils predict, then WATCH a red object go black under blue light (and a white object take the lamp's colour) — the observation directly refutes colour-as-innate-property.

Confront adder-vs-subtractor head-on (IOP 'Understanding colours'): ask 'does the red filter turn all the light red, or just cut out everything except the red already in white light?' — establish filter = selective SUBTRACTOR, and a coloured object = a selective filter.

Sharply separate SUBTRACTIVE pigment/filter behaviour from ADDITIVE light mixing (red + green LIGHT = yellow) — the two are opposite and routinely conflated (70%+ of students wrongly expect red+green spotlights to make brown); teach objects and filters as subtractive.

Order the spectrum by a PHYSICAL quantity (frequency/wavelength), not just 'rainbow order' — red = lowest frequency/longest wavelength through to violet = highest — tying colour to the wave property that dispersion sorts.

Present 'black under blue' as the idealised/limiting case: use saturated pigments and reasonably pure coloured light for a clean effect, and acknowledge real objects look 'very dark', not perfectly black.
Build in accessibility (NASA JPL): for colourblind pupils, label colours with numbers/legends so the assessed reasoning is the absorption model, not hue discrimination.
keyRepresentations: A prism dispersing white light into ROYGBIV (violet refracts most, red least) — paired with a SECOND prism recombining the spectrum back to white.
The visible spectrum ordered by frequency/wavelength (red → violet), labelled with the physical quantity, not just colour names.
Selective-absorption diagram: white light (all colours) strikes a red apple; most colours absorbed (greyed), red reflected to the eye.
The 'same object, different light' comparison: a red object in white light (red) vs the same object in blue light (black).
Filter-as-subtractor diagram: white light through a red filter — red transmitted, the rest absorbed — with a coloured object shown as itself a selective filter.
The IOP Wrong Track / Right Lines paired statements as a refutation representation.
commonMisconceptions: Colour is an innate, fixed property of the object (a red dress 'just is' red), independent of the light illuminating it.
The light merely 'brightens' the object's own colour, rather than the object selecting some frequencies from the light and absorbing the rest.
Colour is ADDED by the light or a filter 'dyes' all light its own colour (adder), rather than SUBTRACTED by selective absorption.
White light is 'just light' / 'normal light', not a mixture of all colours — which undermines both dispersion and colour.
Confusing additive light mixing (red + green LIGHT = yellow) with subtractive pigment/filter behaviour; e.g. expecting red + green spotlights to make brown (documented 70%+ error).
Believing a prism 'adds' or 'creates' colours, rather than separating colours already present in white light.
Predicting a red object under blue light stays red or looks blue/dark-red, instead of black (no red present to reflect).
Forgetting the whole path — perceived colour is the light REACHING THE EYE, which depends on BOTH the pigment and the illuminating light.

learn.summary: For ages 11–12, build understanding that white light is a mixture of all visible colours (ROYGBIV ordered by frequency), that a prism disperses white light because different frequencies refract by different amounts (violet bends most, red least) and a second prism recombines it, that objects appear coloured by selective absorption and reflection (so a red object looks red in white light but near-black in pure blue light), and that filters subtract rather than add colour. The pivotal learning move is predict-observe-reconcile: a learner predicts and explains an object's colour under coloured light, then watches it change, which refutes colour-as-innate-property. Subtractive reasoning is documented as genuinely hard, and additive light mixing must be kept visibly distinct from subtractive pigment/filter behaviour.

activities.title: Colour lab: drive the light, swap the objects
feedback: If a learner predicts the red apple stays red under blue light, point to the absorbed/reflected display: the blue lamp supplies no red, so there is nothing red for the surface to reflect, and the surface absorbs the blue — almost no light reaches the eye, so it looks near-black.

If a learner expects red+blue to blend to purple on the object, distinguish arriving light from returned light: under blue-only light no red arrives, so no red can come back; blending is paint/pigment thinking, not what happens to reflected light.

If a learner says the object just takes the lamp's colour, contrast it with the white shirt (which does look blue because it reflects all colours) versus the red apple (which absorbs blue) — the surface decides what it keeps and returns.

If a learner thinks the prism 'makes' the colours, use the recombination with the second prism: the colours were present all along and dispersion only separates them because each frequency refracts by a different amount.

Name the intuition explicitly ('the object just is that colour and the light brightens it') and contrast it with the model ('white light falls, the surface absorbs some frequencies and reflects the rest to your eye').
activities.rationale: The concept lives in covariation (illuminating light × pigment → perceived colour) and in refutation; a learner-driven simulation supports predict-observe-reconcile and makes absorbed-versus-reflected wavelengths visible. Securing 'what is white light' first via split-and-recombine addresses a documented prerequisite, and keeping additive and subtractive panels distinct targets a routinely conflated pair.
sourceClaims: Objects appear coloured by selective absorption/reflection; the Wrong Track ('object just has that colour, light brightens it') vs Right Lines ('white light falls, object absorbs most frequencies, reflects the rest to the eye') framing; a red dress appears black in blue light; apparent colour depends on both pigment and illuminating light.
A physically adequate concept of WHITE LIGHT is a prerequisite for understanding colour; students conceptualise white light as 'normal light', which impedes colour learning.
Filters are colour SUBTRACTORS — they transmit their own colour and absorb the rest, not dye all light their colour; a coloured object is a selective filter.

Subtractive colour reasoning is genuinely hard: only ~27% correctly predicted a yellow object looks dark under blue light, and over 70% wrongly expected red + green spotlights to make brown (correct: yellow); colour-vision mechanism was less problematic (>85% correct).
learnerActions: Before each reveal, write a prediction AND a reason for what colour an object will appear (e.g. 'red apple under a pure blue lamp').

Dial a light source from white to pure red, green, or blue and shine it on a shelf of objects (red apple, white shirt, black cloth, multicoloured toy); observe which wavelengths are absorbed and which reflect back to the eye.
Watch the red apple turn near-black under pure blue light, and the white shirt take on the lamp's colour; reconcile each observation with your prediction.
Split a white beam through a prism into ROYGBIV, then pass the spectrum through a second prism to recombine it back to white.

Compare the subtractive object/filter behaviour with a separate panel showing overlapping red, green and blue spotlights (additive mixing to yellow/cyan/magenta/white), noting the two rules give opposite results.
Pass white light through coloured filters and describe what is transmitted versus absorbed.
activities.intendedInsight: Perceived colour is light-and-pigment together, not a fixed property of the object: a surface returns only the colours the light supplies and the surface does not absorb. White light is a mixture a prism separates (not creates), and filters/pigments subtract colour while light sources add.

activities.title: Predict-observe-reconcile with a real coloured lamp
feedback: The reason is the diagnostic, not just the colour named: 'red because it's a red object' reveals colour-as-innate; 'black because there's no red light for it to reflect' shows the target model.

If a learner says the red object will take the lamp's colour (blue), use the white control: the white surface reflects all colours so it looks blue, but the red surface absorbs the blue, so it reflects almost nothing and looks near-black.
Reinforce that perceived colour is the light reaching the eye, which depends on both the pigment and the illuminating light.
Treat the near-black result as the idealised limiting case — with real pigment and real lamps the object looks 'very dark' rather than a perfect black.
activities.rationale: A physical investigation with real saturated pigment and reasonably pure coloured light stages the refutation directly and asks the learner to commit to a reasoned prediction, which exposes the misconception before the reveal.
sourceClaims: Objects appear coloured by selective absorption/reflection; the Wrong Track ('object just has that colour, light brightens it') vs Right Lines ('white light falls, object absorbs most frequencies, reflects the rest to the eye') framing; a red dress appears black in blue light; apparent colour depends on both pigment and illuminating light.
learnerActions: Under normal lighting, note that the object is a bright red; then, in a darkened space and before the coloured lamp is switched on, write down the colour you predict it will appear under a pure blue (or green) LED lamp AND your reason.
Switch on the lamp and observe how the object appears (with a saturated red pigment and a narrow-band blue or green lamp it should look very dark, close to black); compare with your prediction.
Repeat with a WHITE object for comparison and note that it takes on the lamp's colour (blue under a blue lamp, green under a green lamp).
State in your own words why the two objects behave differently.
activities.intendedInsight: A discrepant event that colour-as-innate cannot explain: the red object goes near-black because no red light is present to reflect, while the white object reflects whatever colour the lamp provides.

activities.title: Reason about colour: spectrum order, filters, and prisms
feedback: For the spectrum, order by the physical quantity (frequency/wavelength), not just 'rainbow order'.
For red+green spotlights, the answer is yellow; expecting brown conflates subtractive pigment mixing with additive light mixing.
For the red filter, it TRANSMITS red and ABSORBS the rest — it does not dye all the light red.
For the prism, dispersion separates colours already present because each frequency refracts by a different amount; it does not create colour.
Treat 'black' as the idealised limiting case — real pigments and lights give 'very dark', not perfectly black.
activities.rationale: Each learning target maps to a checkable prediction-and-explanation, giving a diagnostic and consolidation route for reasoning research shows is hard; written or selected answers consolidate but do not substitute for the covariation experience of the lab or live demo.
sourceClaims: Subtractive colour reasoning is genuinely hard: only ~27% correctly predicted a yellow object looks dark under blue light, and over 70% wrongly expected red + green spotlights to make brown (correct: yellow); colour-vision mechanism was less problematic (>85% correct).
Filters are colour SUBTRACTORS — they transmit their own colour and absorb the rest, not dye all light their colour; a coloured object is a selective filter.
learnerActions: Order the visible spectrum by increasing frequency (red = lowest frequency/longest wavelength → violet = highest frequency/shortest).
Predict and explain the colour of a red object seen under blue light, and of a white and a black object under the same light.
Match an object plus an illuminating colour to the perceived colour.

Predict what is seen when white light passes through a red filter, and explain why an opaque coloured object behaves like a selective filter, except that it selects the light it reflects rather than the light it transmits.
Predict the result of overlapping red and green spotlights and explain why it is yellow, not brown.
Explain why a prism disperses white light and why a second prism can recombine the spectrum to white.
activities.intendedInsight: Consolidate the subtractive model and separate it from additive light mixing, tying colour order to the physical wave property that dispersion sorts.

constraints: Secure 'what is white light' before colour reasoning: use split-and-recombine with two prisms so 'white = all colours together' is seen, not asserted.
Keep subtractive pigment/filter behaviour visually and conceptually distinct from additive light mixing (red + green LIGHT = yellow); they are opposite rules and routinely conflated.
Present 'black under blue' as the idealised limiting case; use saturated pigments and reasonably pure coloured light, and acknowledge real objects look 'very dark', not perfectly black.
Dispersion rests on refraction as a prerequisite; treat the prism as separating colours already present, never creating them.

Treat qualitative reasoning as the KS3 target (UK statutory home); NGSS MS-PS4-2 is the broader wave reflect/absorb/transmit anchor and has no colour-specific performance expectation, so spectrum/dispersion/subtractive detail is UK-led.

Recognition or selection-only responses (ordering, matching, multiple choice) consolidate and diagnose but do not by themselves elicit independent construction of an explanation; include prediction-with-reason and spoken/written explanation.
For accessibility, label colours with numbers or legends so the assessed reasoning is the absorption model, not hue discrimination (supports colourblind learners).

A static annotated scene is a useful reference and refutation display but cannot let a learner change the light and watch the object flip; use it as a companion to the lab or live demo, not a replacement for the predict-observe move.
A persona/role-play framing (lighting designer, artist) may motivate but does not by itself stage or verify the prediction-and-explanation that demonstrates understanding.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source lists several sources with verified:false (Haagen-Schützenhöfer 2017; IOP 'Understanding colours'; the 2024 TLS colour paper with the ~27% and ~70% figures; NASA JPL; NGSS MS-PS4-2). Quantitative claims (~27% yellow-under-blue, >70% red+green→brown, >85% colour-vision) are reproduced as reported but not independently confirmed here.

The original 'colour-as-innate kills on contact', 'a static picture cannot teach the predict-observe move', '3D adds nothing conceptually', and 'conversation cannot deliver the mechanism' framings are catalog fit judgements, not established comparative-efficacy findings; they have been softened to scoped affordances/limits rather than universal claims.

Physics self-audit: the red-object-under-blue-light-goes-near-black claim is sound for saturated pigment and reasonably pure monochromatic light; kept as an idealised limiting case ('very dark') to avoid overstating a perfect black with real materials and lamps. Dispersion described as frequency-dependent refraction (violet bends most, red least) and as separation not creation, consistent with the recombination demo.

Coherence of Activity 2: the object's red colour is established under normal light before the darkened-space prediction, since the colour cannot be observed in full darkness before the coloured lamp is on.

The KS3 statutory claim was removed from Activity 3 sourceClaims because it anchors curriculum scope rather than the activity's pedagogical rationale; the KS3 anchor remains in constraints. The original probeDeeper double-selection case (a red object viewed through a blue filter in daylight, which also appears dark) is a richer transfer example that could optionally be added to the filter task.

assess.poeTask: Show a bright red object in a blackout, then illuminate it with a pure blue (or green) LED lamp. BEFORE switching on, each child writes down the colour they predict AND their reason. The reason is the diagnostic: 'red because it's a red object' exposes colour-as-innate; 'black because there's no red light for it to reflect' shows the target model. Switch on — the object appears near-black — then have them reconcile prediction with observation. (Use a WHITE object as the control: it looks blue.)
probeDeeper: What colour would a WHITE van look under that same pure blue lamp — and why is that different from the red bus?
Under normal daylight, why does the red bus look red — what happens to the green and blue that also land on it?
A prism spreads white light into a rainbow. Where did those colours come from — did the prism make them? How could you prove your answer?
You look at the red bus through a blue filter in ordinary daylight. What do you see, and is that the same reason or a different one from the blue-lamp case?
assess.correctAnswer: It looks BLACK (very dark). A red object looks red because its surface reflects red light and absorbs the others; under pure blue light there is no red for it to reflect, and it absorbs the blue, so almost no light comes off it to our eyes — it appears black.

errorPatterns.pattern: Colour is an innate property of the object — 'the bus IS red, so it stays red whatever light you shine on it'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Refute with the live demo (red object under a pure blue/green lamp goes black) — a discrepant event they cannot explain with the innate model. Rebuild colour as 'the object returns only the colours the light gives it and its surface doesn't absorb'.
errorPatterns.distractor: It still looks red, because the bus is red.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answers 'red' and, when pushed, insists the paint is red so it can't change; ignores which colours the lamp actually provides.

errorPatterns.pattern: Colours mix additively on the object — 'red bus + blue light = purple bus' — treating illumination like mixing paint.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Separate the two ideas: pigment ABSORBS (subtractive), light sources ADD. On the object, ask 'what colours are arriving, and which does the surface send back?' — under blue-only, no red arrives, nothing red comes back.
errorPatterns.distractor: It looks purple, because red and blue mix.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answers 'purple' or 'a bluey-red'; reasons by blending the object colour with the lamp colour.

errorPatterns.pattern: The object takes on the lamp's colour — 'blue light, so the bus looks blue' — treating the surface as a neutral screen.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast a WHITE object (which does look blue under blue light because it reflects all colours) with the RED object (which absorbs blue). The surface decides what it keeps and what it returns.
errorPatterns.distractor: It looks blue, the same colour as the lamp.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answers 'blue'; does not account for the red surface absorbing the blue.

errorPatterns.pattern: White light is a single 'pure' colourless thing that a prism STAINS or adds colour to, rather than a mixture the prism separates.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use the recombination demo — a second inverted prism turns the spectrum back to white — to show the colours were there all along; dispersion is separation, not creation.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: In probing, says the prism 'colours' the light or 'makes' the rainbow, rather than spreading colours already present because each bends by a different amount.

responseLevels.gap: Says the bus stays red (or takes the lamp's colour, or mixes to purple) and defends it with colour-as-innate or paint-mixing reasoning.
responseLevels.full: Says black/very dark AND explains via selective reflection and absorption (surface reflects only red, which the blue lamp doesn't supply, and absorbs the blue), and transfers correctly — predicts the white van looks blue, and explains a filter or daylight case with the same mechanism.
responseLevels.partial: Gets that the appearance changes and may say 'darker' or 'black', but explains it as a rule ('no red light so it can't be red') without the reflection/absorption mechanism, and cannot reliably transfer to the white-object or filter case.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A red London bus is parked in a dark garage. I switch on a lamp that gives out ONLY pure blue light — no other colours at all. What colour does the bus look now? And explain WHY it looks that colour.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who thinks colour is a fixed property painted onto the object ('it's a red bus, so it's red') answers 'red' and cannot budge. A child who understands colour as selective reflection of the light that is PRESENT reasons that no red is available to reflect, so the object goes dark. The two models give opposite answers to the same question, and tier 2 forces the reflection/absorption mechanism, so 'red' cannot be reached by correct reasoning.
